blocks.text: A cutting insert that survives 60 minutes at 150 m/min does not survive 60 minutes at 200 m/min: it may last only about 19. Raising speed by a third cuts the life by two thirds, and that steep trade is why choosing a cutting speed is an economic decision as much as a mechanical one.

blocks.markdown: A cutting edge wears progressively. Wear is usually measured as the width of the flank wear land $VB$ (mm) on the clearance face; a typical end-of-life criterion for finishing carbide inserts is $VB\approx0.3$ mm. **Tool life** $T$ (min) is the cutting time until the chosen wear limit is reached. It depends strongly on cutting speed $V$ (m/min) because temperature at the tool-chip interface rises with speed, and wear rates rise steeply with temperature.

blocks.title: Taylor's tool life equation
blocks.text: Taylor's equation states $V T^{n} = C$, where $V$ is cutting speed (m/min), $T$ is tool life (min), $n$ is the tool-life exponent and $C$ is a constant equal to the speed that gives a tool life of 1 minute. Both $n$ and $C$ depend on the work material, tool material and, to a lesser degree, feed and depth of cut, and are found by tool-life tests at two or more speeds.

blocks.caption: Taylor tool life: two operating points for the same tool, work and feed

blocks.title: Predicting life at a new speed
blocks.prompt: A carbide insert has $n=0.25$ and gives $T_1=60$ min at $V_1=150$ m/min. Find the constant $C$ and the life at $V_2=200$ m/min.

steps.text: Find $C$ from the known operating point.

blocks.answer: C is about 417 m/min and the life at 200 m/min falls to about 19 minutes.

rows: Life falls very steeply with speed
Tolerates high speed but is brittle
blocks.caption: Typical (not exact) ranges of the Taylor exponent; always use values measured for your own tool and work material

blocks.markdown: Because life falls with speed, a faster cut makes each part sooner but uses more tools and more tool-change stops. Let $C_m$ be the machine plus operator cost rate (currency per min), $t_c$ the time to change a tool (min) and $C_t$ the cost of one cutting edge (currency). Per part, with machining time $t_m$, the number of edges used is $t_m/T$. Adding up the machining, tool-change and tool costs and minimising with respect to $V$ gives a neat result: the optimum tool life depends only on $n$ and on the cost ratios, not on the part.

blocks.caption: Tool life and speed for minimum cost per part (for minimum production time, set $C_t=0$)

blocks.title: Cost-optimal speed
blocks.prompt: Using $n=0.25$ and $C=417.5$ m/min from the carbide insert above, tool change takes $t_c=2$ min, an edge costs $C_t=6$ currency units and the machine rate is $C_m=0.60$ units/min. Find $T_{opt}$ and $V_{opt}$.

steps.text: Compute the equivalent time cost of the edge.
Back-calculate the speed from Taylor's equation.

blocks.answer: The cheapest operation runs the tool for 36 minutes, at about 170 m/min.

blocks.markdown: Why does life fall with speed? At **low speeds** the edge runs cool and wear is mostly mechanical: abrasion by hard particles in the work, and adhesion where fragments of the built-up edge or chip weld to the tool and are torn away, producing flank wear and chipping. At **high speeds** the interface temperature can exceed several hundred degrees Celsius, softening the tool and driving thermally activated mechanisms: diffusion of tool constituents into the flowing chip and chemical reaction, which cut a crater on the rake face, and plastic deformation of the edge. Typical Taylor lines are straight on log-log axes only over the middle range of speeds where one mechanism dominates.

blocks.title: Fast is not always cheap
blocks.text: Minimum cost per part sits at a lower speed (longer tool life) than maximum production rate, because the tool cost term $C_t$ pushes the optimum life up. A shop with a very high machine rate $C_m$ relative to tool cost gets a shorter optimum life and a higher speed, since machine time is the expensive thing.

points: Taylor's equation $VT^n=C$ predicts life at a new speed through $T_2/T_1=(V_1/V_2)^{1/n}$; a small $n$ means life is very sensitive to speed.
The cost-minimising life is $T_{opt}=(1/n-1)(t_c+C_t/C_m)$ and the speed follows from $V_{opt}=C/T_{opt}^{\,n}$.
Minimum production time uses the same formula with $C_t=0$, so it runs faster than minimum cost.
Low speeds wear tools by abrasion and adhesion; high speeds wear them by temperature-driven diffusion, crater wear and plastic deformation.

questions.stem: Which equation is Taylor's tool life relation, with $V$ the cutting speed, $T$ the tool life and $n$, $C$ constants of the tool-work pair?

distractorRationale.a: The ratio form would make life grow with speed, which is the opposite of observed behaviour.
distractorRationale.c: A linear sum would let speed and life trade one for one, which does not match the steep power-law fall in life.
distractorRationale.d: The exponent belongs on the life, not the speed; this form gives the wrong dependence of $T$ on $V$.

questions.explanation: Taylor's equation is $VT^n=C$, a power law that gives straight lines on log-log axes. Life falls as speed rises, and the exponent $n$ controls how steeply.

questions.stem: Which wear mechanism becomes the dominant limit on tool life at very high cutting speeds, where the tool-chip interface is very hot?

options.text: Abrasion by hard inclusions on the flank
Fracture caused by cold built-up edge
Corrosion of the tool by the coolant
Thermally driven diffusion and crater wear on the rake face

questions.correctOptionText: Thermally driven diffusion and crater wear on the rake face

distractorRationale.a: Abrasion is a mechanical wear that occurs at all speeds and is worst at low to moderate speed, where hard particles scratch the flank.
distractorRationale.b: Built-up edge forms at low speeds when the chip is cool enough to weld; it tends to disappear at high speed.
distractorRationale.c: Coolant chemistry is a secondary factor; high-speed life is limited by temperature-activated processes.

questions.explanation: At high speed the interface temperature rises enough for atoms to diffuse from the tool into the chip, cutting a crater on the rake face, and the edge may also soften. Low-speed wear is more abrasive and adhesive in nature.

questions.stem: A carbide tool has Taylor exponent $n=0.2$. At $V=80$ m/min it lasts 45 min. Estimate its life, in minutes, at $V=100$ m/min with the same feed and depth of cut.
questions.explanation: Using $T_2=T_1(V_1/V_2)^{1/n}$ with $1/n=5$ gives $T_2=45(80/100)^5=45(0.32768)=14.7$ min. A 25 percent speed increase cuts life to about a third.

questions.stem: Two tests on the same tool and work material give $T=60$ min at $V=100$ m/min and $T=15$ min at $V=140$ m/min. What is the Taylor exponent $n$?

distractorRationale.b: $0.50$ would result from comparing the speed ratio to the life ratio linearly (a ratio of 4 against a ratio of 1.4 does not give this).
distractorRationale.c: $0.12$ comes from taking natural logs the wrong way round or halving the answer.

questions.explanation: From $V_1T_1^n=V_2T_2^n$, $n=\ln(V_1/V_2)/\ln(T_2/T_1)=\ln(100/140)/\ln(15/60)=(-0.3365)/(-1.3863)=0.243$. The reciprocal, about 4.1, is the exponent used when predicting life from a speed ratio.

questions.stem: A turning insert with $n=0.20$ costs 4.00 currency units per cutting edge. Changing it takes 3.0 min and the machine plus operator rate is 0.50 units/min. Calculate the tool life for minimum cost per part, in minutes.
questions.explanation: The equivalent time cost of the edge is $C_t/C_m=4.00/0.50=8$ min, so $T_{opt}=(1/n-1)(t_c+C_t/C_m)=(5-1)(3+8)=44$ min. The optimum depends only on $n$ and the cost ratios.

questions.stem: Machine and operator labour become more expensive (larger $C_m$) while the tool cost and tool-change time stay the same. What happens to the cost-optimal tool life and cutting speed?

options.text: Optimal life rises and optimal speed falls
Optimal life falls and optimal speed rises
Optimal life falls and optimal speed falls

questions.correctOptionText: Optimal life falls and optimal speed rises

distractorRationale.a: The reverse: tools matter relatively less to cost, so you can afford to wear them out sooner, not later.
distractorRationale.b: The optimum depends on $C_t/C_m$, which changes when $C_m$ changes, so it does not stay fixed.
distractorRationale.d: A shorter life corresponds to a higher speed by Taylor's equation, so speed cannot fall at the same time.

questions.explanation: A larger $C_m$ reduces $C_t/C_m$, so $T_{opt}=(1/n-1)(t_c+C_t/C_m)$ falls. By Taylor's equation shorter life means higher speed, trading cheap tools for faster, cheaper-in-time production.

questions.stem: For a given tool and work material, how does the speed for minimum production time compare with the speed for minimum cost per part?

options.text: It is lower, because the tool changes more often
It is identical, because both minimise cost
It depends on the part length
It is higher, because the tool cost term is ignored

questions.correctOptionText: It is higher, because the tool cost term is ignored

distractorRationale.a: Ignoring tool cost lets the process run hotter and faster; life is shorter, not longer, at the time optimum.
distractorRationale.b: They differ whenever $C_t>0$, since $T_{opt}$ includes $C_t/C_m$ for cost but not for time.
distractorRationale.c: Part length scales machining time but cancels out of the optimum tool life formulas.

questions.explanation: Minimum time uses $T=(1/n-1)t_c$, which omits the $C_t/C_m$ term, so life is shorter and speed higher than for minimum cost. This is why a rush job can justify running the tool harder, at higher tooling cost.

questions.stem: For a tool-work pair with $C=300$ m/min and $n=0.25$, a tool change takes 1.5 min, an edge costs 9.0 currency units and the machine rate is 0.90 units/min. Calculate the cutting speed for minimum cost per part, in m/min.
Contrast how a cutting tool wears at low and at high cutting speed. Name the mechanisms and explain why a plot of life against speed on log-log axes may bend at the extremes.
markingGuide: Low speed: abrasion by hard particles and adhesion (built-up edge, chip welding) causing flank wear and chipping
High speed: high interface temperature causes diffusion and chemical wear (crater on rake face) and plastic deformation of the edge
Temperature rises with speed and thermally activated mechanisms increase steeply
Taylor's equation is a straight line only where one mechanism dominates
At extremes a different mechanism takes over, so the line bends (or life collapses)
questions.explanation: Mechanical wear dominates in cool low-speed cutting, while temperature-driven diffusion and crater wear dominate at high speed. Taylor's straight line is an approximation for the intermediate range where one mechanism governs.

questions.stem: A workshop manager proposes running every turning job as fast as the machine allows to maximise output, and another proposes running slowly to save tooling. Using the idea of cost per part, explain why each is wrong and how an optimum arises. State what determines the optimum tool life.
markingGuide: Cost per part has a machining-time term that falls with speed ($\propto1/V$)
Tool change and tool cost terms rise with speed because life falls as $T=(C/V)^{1/n}$
The sum has a minimum at an intermediate speed
Gives $T_{opt}=(1/n-1)(t_c+C_t/C_m)$ and notes it depends on $n$, $t_c$, $C_t$ and $C_m$
Notes minimum production time is faster than minimum cost, and gives the role of the cost ratio
questions.explanation: Cost per part is the sum of a term that falls with speed and terms that rise with it, so it has an interior minimum. The optimum life depends on $n$ and the tool-change and tool-cost ratios rather than on the part geometry.
